passages.happening:
‘There is another evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily upon mankind’ (verse 1). ‘God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires; but God does not allow him to enjoy them. Instead, a stranger will enjoy them. This is futile and a grievous affliction’ (verse 2).

A man might have a hundred children and live many years. But if he is never satisfied with what he has, and is not even buried with honor, the Teacher says a stillborn child is better off than he (verse 3). That child comes and goes in darkness and is never named (verse 4). It never sees the sun, yet ‘has more rest than that man’ (verse 5), even if he lives two thousand years without enjoying good. ‘Do not all go to the same place?’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 5 ended on a hopeful note: God gives wealth and the power to enjoy it. Chapter 6 turns the coin over. What if God gives the wealth but not the enjoyment? The difference between the two cases cannot be secured by effort. It lies in God's hand.

In the ancient world wealth, many children, a long life and an honorable burial were the recognized marks of a good life. A hundred children and long years were a proverbial picture of success. The Teacher pulls the ground out from under that ideal. Fortunes could pass suddenly to strangers through war, debt, a ruler's seizure, or the lack of an heir, the situation verse 2 describes.

Burial mattered enormously, and to be denied it was a disgrace. That is why the Teacher mentions it: a man could have every outward good and still die unmourned.

The comparison with a stillborn child is meant to shock, and Job used the same picture in his agony (Job 3:11-16). It is a measure of how empty a life of plenty is without joy. It is not a judgment on any child, or on any parent who has lost one.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: The psalm speaks of the people verse 2 describes, ‘whose portion is in this life’ (Psalm 17:14). And Job, in his grief, used the same comparison: “Or why was I not hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees daylight?” (Job 3:16).
passages.hard:
Is it fair for God to give a person wealth and then not allow him to enjoy it?

The Teacher states the problem bluntly in verse 2 and does not solve it.

Some readers take this as a mark of his limited, under-the-sun view: he reports what life looks like without seeing God's hidden purposes, and the book's larger frame (3:11; 12:14) says those purposes exist. Others stress that the Teacher is exposing a false assumption, that possessions carry happiness inside them. Enjoyment does not come bundled with wealth. It is a separate gift, and the person who treats goods as the source of joy will be disappointed even when he has them all. A third observation is simply that the Teacher is honest about something many people experience, and Scripture keeps that honesty instead of hiding it.

The chapter does not accuse God of injustice. It shows that the power to enjoy life is not something anyone can command, and that pushes the reader toward humility and dependence.
passages.asks: Enjoyment is a gift, not a possession. Ask what you have that you are not enjoying, and why. And ask God for the gift of a glad heart in what he has already given.

passages.t: An appetite never filled, and who can tell?
passages.happening:
‘All a man’s labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied’ (verse 7). What advantage does the wise man have over the fool? (verse 8). ‘Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind’ (verse 9).

‘Whatever exists was named long ago, and what happens to a man is foreknown; but he cannot contend with one stronger than he’ (verse 10). More words only mean more futility (verse 11).

The chapter ends with two questions. ‘For who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow? Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
One Hebrew word runs through this chapter, nephesh, which can mean soul, life or appetite. The man lacks nothing his soul desires (verse 2), his soul is not satisfied (verse 3), and his appetite is never filled (verse 7). Verse 9 sets what the eye can see against the wandering of desire, literally the going about of the soul.

Naming something showed authority over it. God names day and night in Genesis 1, Adam names the animals in Genesis 2, and kings renamed conquered rulers. So when verse 10 says that whatever exists was named long ago, a first hearer would hear a claim about God's ordering of all things. The one stronger than man is most naturally God himself.

Many readers treat verses 10 to 12 as the midpoint of the book. The questions of verse 12, who knows and who can tell, set up the second half, where the Teacher shows again and again that people cannot know the future or find out the whole of God's work.
passages.later: James asks the same: ‘You do not even know what will happen tomorrow’ (James 4:14). And the psalm says of human life, ‘Surely every man goes about like a phantom’ (Psalm 39:6).
passages.asks: Life passes like a shadow, and no one can say what comes after. Ask what you are reaching for that the eye cannot see. And ask how you might live today's few days well, trusting the one who knows what you cannot.
